note: Object stories, layers 1-2 only. Written to the read-and-heard standard in BUILD-SPEC-v2.md §6: the spoken words are the printed words, so no line refers to its own medium, none assumes the object is physically in front of the reader, and there is no visual-only structure inside a segment. Every story here is a paraphrase of writing the Museum has already published about that specific object. Nothing is invented: where a fact is not in the source it is not here. Segment ids are the audio chapter boundaries and the skip targets.

coverage.why: Only 12 objects have Museum-authored interpretive writing anywhere. The other 116 have a cataloguer's physical description and nothing else, and §6 forbids that standing in for a story. Writing them requires either third-party natural-history sources or a commission - see docs/prototype-findings.md.

museum-blaschka-page.citation: Le Grice R. The Blaschka Collection. Canterbury Museum.
museum-blaschka-page.note: Twelve collection highlights, each with a paragraph of interpretive writing, an accession number and a Blaschka model number. Paraphrased here, not reproduced. Several of its identifications differ from the collection record; where they do, the difference is recorded on the story.

1884.137.33.headline: Portuguese man o' war
1884.137.33.identification: The Museum's page gives this as Physalia physalis. The collection record says Physalia pelagica.

segments.heading: Look closely
segments.text:
The whole thing is glass. It stands about 28 centimetres tall. Two long tentacles hang from it, and seven shorter ones. You can count them. It rests on a green wire rod.

This is a Portuguese man o' war. In New Zealand waters it is better known as the bluebottle. Its other name comes from its resemblance to an 18th-century Portuguese sailing warship.

segments.heading: Not one animal
segments.text:
A man o' war is related to true jellyfish. But it is not one. And it is not a single creature either.

It is a colonial organism, made up of many individual organisms called zooids. Zooids stay connected as they grow. Each one has its own specialised job. None of them can survive alone.

segments.heading: A float, and a sail
segments.text:
Look at the top section. In a living man o' war that part does two jobs at once. It is a float, and it is a sail. They travel on the currents and the wind.

Every man o' war is either left-handed or right-handed, depending on which way that sail curves.

The tentacles below can reach ten metres. They catch small crustaceans and fish.

segments.heading: Look closely
segments.text:
A shallow glass bell, fringed with fine tentacles all the way around the rim. Beneath it hang four longer arms with frilled edges.

Near the top of the bell are four crescent shapes, picked out here in red and pink. Those are the reproductive organs. On a moon jellyfish they are very nearly the only coloured part. The rest of the animal is white, or no colour at all.

segments.heading: How it eats
segments.text:
The short tentacles around the rim sting, and hold what they catch still. The four long frilled arms then carry the food up to the mouth.

A full-grown bell can reach 45 centimetres across.

segments.heading: Blooms, and going backwards
segments.text:
Moon jellyfish sometimes gather in enormous numbers in one stretch of sea. These gatherings are called blooms, and they appear to be happening more often. Part of the reason is that the animals which eat moon jellyfish, among them turtles and sharks, are in trouble themselves.

There is one more thing. A moon jellyfish can go backwards through its own life cycle, and return to a stage it had already passed.

segments.heading: Look closely
segments.text:
A heavy white bell, shaped something like a mushroom, with eight thick arms gathered below it.

This is a giant. Large ones reach 150 centimetres. Its other name is the dustbin-lid jellyfish, and that is the size being described.

segments.heading: Frills full of holes
segments.text: The eight arms are covered in frills, and the frills are full of tiny openings. The animal draws water through them and strains out its food. What it is straining for is plankton.

segments.heading: Where they gather
segments.text:
Barrel jellyfish are common in the eastern Atlantic and the Mediterranean. In the warmer months they swarm together close to shore, and they often end up washed onto beaches.

They are the favourite meal of the leatherback turtle.

segments.heading: Look closely
segments.text:
Brown markings run outward across the top of the bell, dividing it into segments. They look like the face of a compass, and that is where the name comes from.

The rest of the bell is translucent, somewhere between yellow and white. At full size it is about 25 centimetres across.

segments.heading: Two kinds of arm
segments.text:
There are two different things hanging underneath, and they do different jobs.

The four broad arms are for feeding. The many slender tentacles are the weapons. They carry stinging cells, which disable prey and defend the animal against the things that hunt it. Sunfish and leatherback turtles both eat compass jellyfish.

segments.heading: A colour the glass does not show
segments.text:
The living animal is usually a distinct purple. The model is not, so this is one place where the glass does not tell you everything.

It is a small jellyfish. It grows to around 12 centimetres across, and it is found in warm seas all over the world.

segments.heading: Two names, one habit
segments.text:
This animal is called the mauve stinger, and it is also called the night-light jellyfish.

The second name is the more interesting one. It glows in the dark. The word for making your own light is bioluminescence, and this jellyfish does it.

segments.heading: Count the ribs
segments.text:
Ridges run out from the centre of the bell towards the rim, studded with small warty bumps. Those ridges are what separate this animal from its closest relatives, and they are what gave it its name.

The bell reaches about 40 centimetres across.

segments.heading: The pale yellow is real
segments.text:
The soft yellow in this model is not a decision the glassmaker made for effect. It matches the written scientific description of the animal, and the colour comes from its reproductive organs. How strong it is depends on whether the animal is male or female.

This one goes by several names. Many-ribbed jellyfish is one. Crystal jelly and water jelly are others. Like the man o' war, it is a relative of the true jellyfish rather than one of them.

1884.137.61.headline: Hula-skirt siphonophore
1884.137.61.identification: The Museum's page gives this as Physophora hydrostatica, and numbers it 1884.137.61b. The collection record says Physophora magnifica and holds no sub-part suffix.

segments.heading: Look closely
segments.text:
The top is a stack of clear bells, sitting one on another. Below them, a ring of short tentacles hangs out and down, and that ring is where the name comes from. It looks like a skirt.

Those tentacles are how the animal catches plankton.

segments.heading: Many animals, one body
segments.text:
A siphonophore is not an individual. It is a colony of parts called zooids, which stay joined together as they grow.

Each zooid has one job. Some feed, some reproduce, some swim. All of them work for the whole, and not one of them could live on its own.

segments.heading: Rising and sinking
segments.text:
At the bottom of the float is a small pore that lets gas out. That is how the animal controls whether it rises or sinks.

It lives deep down, where no sunlight reaches. The only light there is light that living things make for themselves.

segments.heading: A sea slug that swims
segments.text:
Two wing-shaped lobes stand out from the body. Almost every other sea slug crawls along the seabed. This one does not touch it. It swims in open water, and it beats those two lobes to do it.

It is called the sea angel, and also the sea cherub.

segments.heading: What the name hides
segments.text:
The name suggests something gentle. The animal is not.

It hunts. It shoots out a long feeding tube covered in hooks and teeth, and takes hold of its prey with it. What it mostly eats is sea butterflies, which are swimming sea snails.

segments.heading: The shell is not a home
segments.text:
The white curved shell is the thing everyone notices. It is not what it looks like. This animal is an octopus, and the shell is not the sort a snail lives in.

She makes it herself, and she uses it two ways. It helps her control how she floats, and it is where she keeps her eggs.

segments.heading: Two sizes
segments.text:
The difference between the sexes is extreme. A male grows to about 2 centimetres. A female can be more than ten times that.

Argonauts live out in open water, in tropical and warm seas around the world.

segments.heading: Riding on jellyfish
segments.text: An argonaut will take hold of a jellyfish and stay with it. The jellyfish becomes three things at once. It is cover from anything hunting the octopus. It is a way of getting about. And it is food, because the argonaut eats the jellyfish a little at a time, and eats what the jellyfish has caught as well.

1884.137.8.headline: Melibe nudibranch
1884.137.8.identification: The Museum's page gives this as Melibe viridis. The collection record says Melibe fimbriata.

segments.heading: An odd shape, for a reason
segments.text:
Along each side of the body are paired lobes, and at the head end is something most sea slugs do not have. It is a wide hood.

That hood is the mouth.

segments.heading: Casting a net
segments.text:
Most sea slugs feed with a rasping tongue called a radula. This group has none. The hood does the work instead.

The animal opens the hood wide, throws it forward over the seabed, and draws it back closed. Anything small enough is caught inside. Small crustaceans are what it is after.

1884.137.70.headline: Sandy creeplet
1884.137.70.identification: The Museum's page gives this as Epizoanthus couchii. The collection record says Zoanthus couchii.

segments.heading: Look closely
segments.text:
This is a colony, not a single animal. Each member is a small sea anemone, and they grow joined together.

One member can carry as many as 32 tentacles. Each tentacle is translucent, with a bright white rounded tip.

segments.heading: How it disappears
segments.text:
Disturb this animal and the tentacles pull in. Once they are in, there is very little left to see.

It lives fixed to rocks and shells, sometimes in large spreading masses, around the coasts of Britain, Ireland, France and Spain. Its body is often covered in a layer of sand, which is where the name comes from.

1884.137.93.headline: Dorid nudibranch
1884.137.93.identification: The Museum's page gives this as Dendrodoris nigra. The collection record says Actinodoris australis.

segments.heading: Look closely
segments.text: A broad flat body with two horns at the front and a rosette of fine gills at the back. It grows to between 4 and 7 centimetres.

segments.heading: The colour changes with age
segments.text:
This species does not keep one colour. A young one is pink or orange. An adult is black.

It is a very common animal. It lives in the intertidal zone, under stones in shallow sandy pools, in warm and temperate seas nearly everywhere. The one part of the world it is missing from is the tropical American coast.

panelsNote: Eleven panels and endings, from docs/group-panels.md. Two faults the draft's own notes identified are fixed here. Idiom no longer carries a sentence on its own — the plain clause states the meaning and the figure follows as a bonus, which is what §7 needs for translation. And no ending asserts what the reader just did: §11 says arriving by code is the normal case, so every panel and ending has to read correctly for someone who landed here directly and will read no other page. The chain between pages is the second reading, never the first.

jellyfish.panel: A jellyfish is a bell of almost pure water, pulsing, trailing threads that sting. That is the whole design. Here it runs from one the size of a dinner plate down to others you could rest on a fingertip — and three times over, the same animal shown as male, as female, and as an infant.
jellyfish.ending: Every animal on this page is a jellyfish. The next page opens with the most famous jellyfish of all, which turns out not to be one.

floating-colonies.panel: These are colonies. Each one looks like a single animal and is not. Each is many separate individuals, joined into one drifting body. Some of them sting, some digest, some reproduce, and not one could live alone. They float in open water, and the wind and the current decide where they go.
floating-colonies.ending: These animals go where the water goes. The next page belongs to animals that solved the same problem — open water, nowhere to hide — a completely different way.

see-through-swimmers.panel: In open water there is nowhere to hide. So these animals, unrelated and from different branches of the tree, arrived at the same two answers. Become invisible, and swim by beating something. Glass is the only material that could ever have shown you the first one.
see-through-swimmers.ending: Transparency is a defence. On the next page a body so plain it looks like nothing much hides one of the strangest facts in this collection.

sea-squirts-and-salps.panel: They look like nothing much: a jelly sack, pumping seawater in one opening and out the other. But somewhere in the life cycle of every one of them sits a swimming, tadpole-shaped animal with a stiff rod down its back. Of everything in this collection, these are your closest relatives.
sea-squirts-and-salps.ending: This page holds both kinds of life. Some of these animals drift; the rest are fixed to a rock. Everything from here on lives on the seabed.

cephalopods.panel: Molluscs that gave up the shell and became hunters instead: arms, suckers, and an eye very nearly as good as yours. The argonaut is here twice, deliberately. The female builds a paper cradle for her eggs. The male is barely a centimetre long.
cephalopods.ending: Losing the shell bought speed, arms and eyes. On the next page, the same decision was paid for very differently.

sea-slugs.panel: Take a snail's shell away and it needs another answer. These fourteen found several: poison, colour loud enough to work as a warning, stinging cells stolen from the animals they eat. One goes further. It steals the working parts out of the algae it eats, keeps them alive, and runs partly on sunlight.
sea-slugs.ending: Every animal so far has moved under its own power. From here, most of them stay where they are.

sea-anemones.panel: An anemone is a ring of poisoned tentacles on top of a stomach, on top of a foot. That is the entire animal. These nineteen show how far one simple idea can be pushed. It is the largest group here, and that is not an accident. Anemones were the great Victorian obsession, and the one thing nobody could keep alive in a jar.
sea-anemones.ending: One animal, nineteen ways. Next: what happens when that same animal stops being one and becomes thousands.

corals-and-sea-fans.panel: Every branch, fan and stony twig on this page is a city. Each is thousands of tiny anemone-like animals sharing a single skeleton. That is how they grow like plants without being plants, and why a coral can be red, blue, feathered, or turned entirely to stone.
corals-and-sea-fans.ending: These built upward from the rock. The last two pages of the sea belong to animals that went the other way, down into it.

sea-cucumbers-and-stars.panel: A sausage, a feather and a star. Nothing about these eight looks related, and that is the point. Count in fives, look for hundreds of tiny water-powered feet, and they turn out to be built on a starfish's plan. There is not one starfish among the models here, and the reason is the reason this collection exists: a starfish dries and keeps. These do not.
sea-cucumbers-and-stars.ending: Built like a starfish, shaped like anything but. The next page is a whole group defined the same way — by a solution rather than a family.

worms.panel: A worm is not a family. It is a solution — a long soft body for pushing through sediment — arrived at separately by four different branches of the animal kingdom. Three here hide the body in a tube altogether and put out a crown so fine it was long mistaken for a flower.
worms.ending: That is the last of the sea. One page remains, and not one animal on it ever went there.

never-went-to-sea.panel: Ten of the models in this collection never saw salt water: garden slugs, a Roman snail cut open to show its insides, a leech from a pond. The Blaschkas supplied classrooms as well as museums, and a lecture room needed the animal in the cabbage patch as much as the one in the Bay of Naples.
